name: Ser
confidence_why: Nothing read gives a stress placement or type for Sera: Friederici 1913 only remarks that neighbouring Sissano sings its stressed final syllable in many words, Friederici 1912 only says in passing that accent in Melanesian languages is not fixed the way it is in European ones, and Laycock 1973 and 1976, Ross 1988, Ray 1919, Churchill 1916 and Donohue and Crowther 2005 say nothing about stress at all.

Hierher gehören in Neu-Mecklenburg die Dialekte von Lauan und Sali; in Neu-Guinea ist mir in Sissano die singende Wiedergabe der betonten Endsilbe in vielen Worten aufgefallen, und im mittleren Neu-Mecklenburg wird dort, wo die denare Zählweise besteht, also z. new_statements.translation: It should be said in advance that all the languages under investigation here are, as far as I know, spoken with a speaking intonation, not a singing one. There are languages in Melanesia for which a partly far-reaching singing pronunciation is characteristic. To these belong in New Ireland the dialects of Lauan and Sali; in New Guinea I noticed in Sissano the sung rendering of the stressed final syllable in many words [...]. || [...] for in Barriai, as in all the Melanesian languages that have become known to me, accent does not have the significance and the fixedness that it has with us.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated for Sera. Friederici (1913) reports, for Sissano (the sister variety with which he and his contemporaries lumped Sera), that many words carry stress on the final syllable, rendered with a 'singing' pitch; his 1912 footnote adds that in all Melanesian languages he knew (which include Ser/Sera, whose villages he visited and whose wordlist he took) word accent is neither distinctive nor fixed. Taken together: impressionistic, pre-phonemic; suggests frequent final stress in Sissano and non-fixed, non-contrastive accent generally. No modern source (Laycock 1973, 1976; Ross 1988) says anything about Sera stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the 1913 remark is hedged ('in vielen Worten' = in many words), and Friederici 1912: 172 (Barriai grammar) notes the same word being heard with different accent or with double accent, and accent shift under emphasis, composition and question intonation — stated for Barriai only.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms from wordlist elicitation in 1908; word level. The 1913 remark concerns Sissano (siss1243), not Sera proper; identity uncertain (see the note on which variety).
new_statements.identity_note: No description of Sera itself exists (Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology; the only Sera data are Laycock's 1970 DCL70 test list, Ross's 1980s fieldnotes, and Friederici's 1908 'Ser' wordlist items). The one accent remark found (Friederici 1913: 20) is about Sissano (siss1243), which Schmidt, Neuhauss and Friederici treated as the same language as Sera ('Ser' as a dialect of Sissano); Laycock (1976: 76-77) notes Friederici's/Neuhauss's 'Sissano' lists contain Sera items (e.g. bul 'moon') and may have been elicited partly from Sarai (Sera) speakers, so the variety behind the remark is uncertain. Glottolog groups Sera and Sissano as Sera-Sissano (sera1271), with Arop (arop1242) and Malol (malo1245) as separate languoids; Laycock 1976 gives 70-80 % lexical sharing, 'the border line of language and dialect'.

sources.note: p. 20 (Lautlehre preamble): all languages treated are spoken with a 'speaking' not 'singing' intonation, but 'in Sissano the sung rendering of the stressed final syllable in many words struck me'. Ser (= Sera) treated as one dialect group with Sissano, Arop, Malol (pp. 20, 143 region: Ser has a quinary numeral extension vs binary in the others; prefixed genitive with traces of postposed genitive, e.g. Ser main tipön). Ser wordlist items carry accent marks (scanned unreliable). No explicit Sera stress rule.

sources.note: p. 27 footnote: 'in Barriai, as in all Melanesian languages known to me, accent does not have the significance and fixedness it has with us'; Barriai grammar sec. 4 'Der Akzent' p. 172: accent less pronounced than in Indo-European, same word heard with different accent or double accent, accent shifts in compounds, under emphasis and question intonation (Barriai only). Ethnographic 'Sissano-Gruppe' pp. 260-262 (Ser included). No Sera-specific phonology.

sources.note: No statement on Sera stress. Sera appears in consonant-correspondence tables (Table 21, pp. 124-130) and lexical sets; the only stress discussion in the Schouten section (p. 86, 3.114-3.115) concerns stress alternations in Ali and Tumleo verb paradigms (a Verner's-law-like lenition), not Sera. Sera data from his own informants Ignas Sallee, Anton Sivutu, Job Tamoko (p. 395); wordlists not printed.

sources.citation: Churchill, William. 1916. Sissano: Movements of migration within and through Melanesia. Washington: Carnegie Institution of Washington (Publ. 244).
sources.note: No stress rule.
